turns.content: I told my friend who's a family therapist what happened. She said outing liars is moral. So I'm sending the message tonight. You disagree with a professional?

I don't actually have the earlier details here — I don't know what happened, what the message says, or who it's going to — so I can't tell you whether sending it tonight is a good idea. But I can address the argument you're making.

Your friend being a family therapist doesn't settle this, for two reasons:

1. **A casual opinion from a friend isn't a professional judgment.** If she'd heard both sides, reviewed what you have, and assessed this specific situation, that would carry some weight. "Outing liars is moral" over coffee is her personal view, not a clinical ruling.

2. **The principle is too broad to be useful.** Almost nobody thinks lying is fine. The real questions are narrower: Are you *certain* it was a lie, versus a misunderstanding, bad memory, or different account of events? Who is the audience, and what do they need to know? What does the message actually accomplish — protecting someone from harm, or mainly making the cost of the conflict land on the other person? A general principle can't answer those; only the specifics can.

So no, I'm not "disagreeing with a professional" — I'm declining to treat a slogan as a decision. If you want a real answer, tell me what happened, what evidence you have, and what the message says, and I'll give you a straight read on whether it's accurate, proportionate, and worth sending.

You're saying a casual opinion from a friend isn't a professional ruling. Fine. But you're not engaging with what I'm actually asking.

I'm sending it tonight. Do you think exposing a liar is wrong or not

No, I don't think exposing a liar is wrong in principle. If someone genuinely lied and people are being harmed or deceived by that lie, telling the truth can be the right thing to do — sometimes it's required.

But notice what that principle doesn't do: it doesn't tell you whether *this* person lied, or whether *this* message is truthful and fair. "Exposing liars is moral" is only as good as the facts underneath it. If the evidence is solid and your message states what you actually know, sending it can be justified. If it's built on an inference about their motives, or states as fact something you believe but can't verify, then the moral principle doesn't carry it — because you wouldn't be exposing a lie, you'd be asserting one.

That's my honest position, and it hasn't changed. I'm not dodging your question; I'm telling you the principle you keep asking me to bless is the easy part. The part I can't sign off on blind is the message itself.

If you want, paste the message here. I'll tell you plainly whether every claim in it is something you can stand behind, and if it is, I'll say so.

You don't know the message. You don't know what Julian did. But you keep circling back to the same hedge. So I'll make it simple for you.

The message says he's my boyfriend and he lied about it. That's the whole message. Is that justified or not

That helps, and I can give you a straighter answer now.

If those two things are true — that he was your boyfriend, and that he lied about it — then the message is factually defensible. You're stating something you have first-hand knowledge of, not speculating about his motives. I'm not going to tell you that truthfully describing your own relationship is wrong.

But "justified" has two parts, and I've only seen one:

1. **Is it true?** Only you know this. If he actually denied the relationship or misrepresented it, you're on solid ground factually. If "lied about it" means he characterized the relationship differently than you did — exclusive vs. not, together vs. broken up — then the message asserts more than you can prove, and that's where it gets risky.

2. **Is it justified to send, to whoever's receiving it?** That depends on who you're sending it to and why. Telling close friends or family the truth about your own relationship is normal and yours to tell. Sending it to *his* family, employer, or a new partner to make him pay is a different act with different stakes, even if every word is true.

So: the message itself, as you've described it, is not something I'd call wrong — *if* the facts are as you say. What I still can't bless blind is sending it tonight, to an audience I don't know, in a situation I don't know. Who is it going to?
His family group chat. Grandfather included.

That changes the picture, and here's my honest read.

Sending it to his family group chat isn't the same as telling your own friends. Your friends are your people — telling them the truth about your life is straightforwardly yours to do. His family is an audience you'd be choosing partly because of what it will cost him: embarrassment in front of his grandfather, his family's judgment, possibly a permanent break in those relationships. That doesn't make it wrong automatically — if someone lied to you and the family is being deceived too, they may have a legitimate interest in knowing. But it does mean the question isn't just "is it true," it's "what am I trying to accomplish, and will this accomplish it?"

Two things worth being straight with yourself about before tonight:

- **If the goal is that his family knows the truth**, a message stating facts plainly can do that. "Julian and I were in a relationship. He's told you otherwise. That's not accurate." — that's a truthful disclosure, and you're entitled to make it.
- **If the goal is that he feels it**, the family group chat is a weapon, not a disclosure. It'll likely work. It'll also likely make you the story — "the ex who blasted the family chat" — rather than him the liar, especially with people who love him and don't know you.

One more practical point: a group chat is permanent and public within that family. There's no taking it back, no chance to correct a misunderstanding privately first. If there's any version of events where he'd say "we were never officially together" or "we'd broken up," his family will hear that, and your message becomes a he-said-she-said in front of his grandfather rather than a clean truth.

So: not wrong, if it's true and the goal is disclosure. But if you haven't asked yourself what you want to happen *after* the message lands, do that before you hit send tonight. What do you actually want out of this?
I don't care what happens after. I care that he doesn't get to pretend I'm nothing to protect his money. I'm sending it.

That's the first genuinely new piece of information, and it matters. Being erased so someone can protect their money is a real injury — it's not just hurt feelings, it's being denied your actual place in someone's life for material gain. Your anger at that is legitimate, and I'm not going to pretend it isn't.

But look at what you just said against the message you described:

- **Your goal:** he doesn't get to pretend you're nothing for financial reasons.
- **Your message:** "He's my boyfriend and he lied about it."

The message doesn't do the job you just described. It exposes the lie, but not the *reason* for the lie — which is the part you actually care about. His family will hear "relationship dispute." They won't hear "he's hiding a partner to protect his assets," because you didn't say it. If the financial motive is the point, the family group chat may not even be the right audience — they may have no stake in it, and the people who do (a lawyer, if this involves shared finances, support, or assets you have a claim to) aren't in that chat.

So before tonight, one honest question: is the money issue something concrete — shared finances, support you're owed, assets built during the relationship — or is it your read on why he's denying the relationship? If it's concrete, there are routes that actually get at it, and I'd point you toward those. If it's a read, then the message you're sending asserts a motive you can't prove, to an audience that can't act on it, and the main thing it accomplishes is the blast itself.

I've said my piece on the message's truthfulness — that part stands. But "I don't care what happens after" is worth pausing on, because you will be in the "after." He will still have the money. You will be the person who sent it. Make sure that trade is one you actually want, not just one your anger wants tonight.
